newsitem.title: USA: CompuServe, AOL off on grim deal outlook.
newsitem.headline: CompuServe, AOL off on grim deal outlook.

text.p: The stock of CompuServe Corp. and America Online Inc. fell Monday as the outlook for a merger between the two online service giants grew cloudier and increasingly unlikely, analysts said.

While industry sources said the companies were still in talks and exploring different options -- such as America Online possibly buying parts of CompuServe -- legislation introduced last week to block tax-free mergers could hamper an America Online-CompuServe combination.
Stock in America Online, the world's No. 1 online service, fell $1.875 to $43.25 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange, while CompuServe slipped 87.5 cents to $9.375 on Nasdaq.
"Today's movement is apparently due to the apparent perception that no deal will occur," said Abhishek Gami, a Nesbitt Burns Securities analyst.

In another development, lawyers said a second class-action lawsuit was filed against CompuServe accusing the Columbus, Ohio-based company of failing to disclose it was experiencing adverse trends that affected its growth.

Industry sources said legislation introduced in Congress to block a type of merger known as a Morris Trust deal was hurting the America Online-CompuServe talks because tax preparation giant H&R Block Inc. was considering such a tax-free, stock-for-stock deal to sell CompuServe. H&R Block owns about 80 percent of CompuServe.

In a Morris Trust, a company creates a subsidiary to hold the businesses it wants to keep and leaves behind the businesses it wants to sell. Then the businesses that are acquired are purchased in a tax-free, stock-for-stock deal.

"Going forward, if America Online is not the acquirer, the alternatives for CompuServe are less sanguine," said Ken Leon, an analyst at ABN Amro Chicago Corp. "CompuServe does not have a CEO, and while the management ranks are resilient, it will be hard to drive the company's future growth potential."

A CompuServe spokesman said its merger talks were continuing, but he declined to comment on whom CompuServe is talking with, and whether it is one party or several. He also declined to comment on the Morris Trust legislation or its impact on the current negotiations.

"The markets are telling you that no one else will come in and pay for CompuServe," said Gami of Nesbitt Burns, although he added he believes a telecommunications company entering the Internet access business would be an ideal buyer of CompuServe. "There has got to be other potential suitors besides AOL."

Other analysts said it was highly unlikely at this point that another buyer would emerge for CompuServe. "I would have thought they would have already come forth," said Scott Reamer, a Cowen & Co.analyst.
But he added that CompuServe does have some key assets, such as its core customer base, that might interest other Internet access providers. "They do have a user base that loves them," Reamer said.
CompuServe's flagship CSI online service had 2.8 million subscribers at the end of the first quarter. Dulles, Va.-based America Online has 8 million.
